passages.t: Moab's cities ruined in a night
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Moab’ (verse 1). Ar and Kir, two of its chief cities, are ruined, each destroyed in a single night.

‘Dibon goes up to its temple to weep at its high places’ (verse 2). Moab wails over Nebo and Medeba. ‘Every head is shaved, every beard is cut off’ (verse 2). People wear sackcloth in the streets and wail on the rooftops and in the squares (verse 3). Heshbon and Elealeh cry out, heard as far as Jahaz, and even Moab's soldiers cry out and tremble (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The oracles against the nations move from Babylon, Assyria and Philistia across the Dead Sea to Moab on the east. Chapters 15 and 16 are one oracle, the longest against any of Judah's small neighbors.

Moab lay on the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, with rich grazing and farmland it contested with Israel for centuries. Genesis traces the Moabites to Lot, Abraham's nephew, and Ruth, David's great-grandmother, was a Moabite. Relations were often hostile. Around 840 BC King Mesha of Moab threw off Israel's rule, and his victory inscription, the Mesha Stele, found at Dibon in 1868, names several towns in this chapter, including Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Jahaz and Horonaim. In Isaiah's time Moab, like Judah, paid tribute to Assyria.

The chapter is a catalogue of ancient mourning customs: shaved heads and beards, sackcloth, wailing in the streets and on the flat rooftops where families spent much of their time. The temple and high places at Dibon were Moabite shrines, most likely to Chemosh, Moab's god. In the crisis the people go up to weep before their own gods.

The disaster cannot be tied with certainty to a known event. Suggestions include an Assyrian campaign in the late eighth century BC, raids by desert tribes, or an earlier attack whose oracle Isaiah takes up and applies again (16:13 calls it a word spoken earlier).
passages.later: Kings tells how ‘after the death of Ahab, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel’ (2 Kings 3:5). A century after Isaiah, Jeremiah reused many lines of this oracle for a new judgment on Moab: ‘I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab’ (Jeremiah 48:31).
passages.asks: In their crisis, Moab's people went up to weep before gods that could not help. Ask where you run first when disaster strikes. And ask what it would look like to grieve your losses before the living God.

passages.t: A heart that cries out over Moab
passages.happening:
Then a surprising line: ‘My heart cries out over Moab’ (verse 5). Her refugees flee as far as Zoar and Eglath-shelishiyah. They climb the slope of Luhith weeping, and lament on the road to Horonaim.

The waters of Nimrim are dried up, the grass withered, and nothing green is left (verse 6). So they carry their wealth and belongings across the Brook of the Willows (verse 7). Their outcry echoes to Moab's borders, to Eglaim and Beer-elim (verse 8).

‘The waters of Dimon are full of blood’ (verse 9), but more is coming: a lion upon the fugitives of Moab and on those left in the land.
passages.hearers:
The place names trace a map of the disaster. Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Nebo and Medeba lay on the northern tableland. Zoar lay at the south end of the Dead Sea. The Brook of the Willows is probably a stream on Moab's southern border. The refugees flee south, which suggests an invader from the north. Dimon is probably a play on Dibon, echoing the Hebrew word for blood, dam.

The first hearers in Judah might have expected to cheer Moab's fall. Moab was an old rival. Instead the oracle grieves. It shows that God's judgment on the nations is not something for Judah to gloat over. The next chapter will even raise the question of Moab finding refuge in Zion.
passages.later: Ezekiel hears God ask, ‘Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?’ (Ezekiel 18:23). Jeremiah grieves in the same way, ‘I will weep for you, O vine of Sibmah’ (Jeremiah 48:32).
passages.hard:
Why would a prophet of Israel grieve over Moab, Israel's enemy?

Readers have puzzled over the tenderness of verse 5 and of 16:9-11. Some think the speaker is the prophet himself, moved by the scale of suffering even among enemies. Others think the voice is God's, and see a judge who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. A few scholars read the lament as a formal dirge that need not express personal feeling, since mourning songs over enemies could also be mocking. The sustained detail and the repetition in chapter 16 lead most readers to take the grief as genuine.

On that reading, the oracle shows that judgment can be just and still grievous, and that God's people are to feel it rather than cheer it. It gives no one leave to rejoice over the suffering of any people, enemy or not.
passages.asks: The prophet's heart cried out for a people his nation counted as enemies. Ask whose suffering you have been glad of because they were on the other side. And ask what it would take for your heart to cry out for them.
